content: There are numerous established airway clearance techniques (ACTs) used to manage respiratory health in individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF). However, no single technique has been proven superior to others. Previous Cochrane Reviews have demonstrated short-term benefits of ACTs in facilitating mucus transport, but there is no evidence to support their long-term efficacy. Exercise has been proposed as an alternative ACT, as it may generate shearing forces within the lung tissue, promoting mucociliary clearance and aiding in the removal of thickened secretions. Recent findings indicate that some individuals with CF are substituting traditional ACTs with exercise, although no formal recommendations exist to support this practice. Furthermore, one of the top research priorities identified by the CF community is determining whether exercise can replace other ACTs. A systematic review of the evidence regarding the safety and efficacy of exercise as an ACT could help individuals with CF make informed decisions about incorporating exercise into their treatment regimens, potentially reducing their overall treatment burden. This review is particularly timely given the evolving landscape of CF care, driven by the introduction of highly effective small molecule therapies that are transforming disease management. The primary objective of this review was to compare the effects of exercise with other ACTs on respiratory function and other clinical outcomes in individuals with CF, while also assessing potential adverse effects associated with exercise as an ACT. On February 28, 2022, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, which includes data from electronic databases and manual searches of journals and conference abstracts. Additional searches were performed in online clinical trial registries on February 15, 2022. Authors of studies awaiting classification or with potentially eligible abstracts were contacted for further information on February 1, 2021. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared exercise to another ACT in individuals with CF, with a minimum of two treatment sessions. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the risk of bias in the included studies. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach, and study investigators were contacted for additional relevant information. Four RCTs were included in the review, involving a total of 86 participants aged 7 to 41 years, with varying degrees of disease severity (FEV1 ranging from 54% to 95%). Two trials employed a cross-over design, while the other two used a parallel design. One trial included participants hospitalized for acute respiratory exacerbations, whereas the other three involved clinically stable individuals. All four trials compared exercise either alone or in combination with another ACT, but the heterogeneity of the interventions precluded pooling of results. The certainty of the evidence was rated as very low due to small sample sizes and high or unclear risks of bias across all domains. Exercise versus Active Cycle of Breathing Technique (ACBT): One cross-over trial with 18 participants compared exercise alone to ACBT. No significant changes in FEV1 (the primary outcome) were observed from baseline, although a transient increase in FEV1 was noted in the exercise group before returning to baseline after 30 minutes. The evidence was of very low certainty, leaving it unclear whether exercise had any effect on FEV1. Similar findings were reported for other lung function measures. No adverse events occurred during exercise sessions, but the evidence was again of very low certainty. It remains uncertain whether ACBT was perceived as more effective or preferred over exercise. A secondary outcome, 24-hour sputum volume, was lower in the exercise group compared to ACBT. Other outcomes, such as exercise capacity, quality of life, adherence, hospitalizations, and the need for additional antibiotics, were not reported. Exercise plus Postural Drainage and Percussion (PD&P) versus PD&P alone: Two trials with a total of 55 participants compared exercise combined with PD&P to PD&P alone. One trial reported a greater increase in FEV1% predicted with PD&P alone after two weeks, while the other trial reported a greater increase with the combination of exercise and PD&P after six months, though no data were provided for the PD&P-only group. The certainty of the evidence was very low, making it unclear whether exercise combined with PD&P improves FEV1. Other lung function measures showed no clear evidence of benefit. One trial reported no difference in exercise capacity (measured as maximal work rate) after two weeks. No adverse events were reported in the trials. Adherence was high, with 100% of PD&P sessions and 96% of exercise sessions completed in one trial. There were no differences between groups in 24-hour sputum volume or mean duration of hospitalization, although the six-month trial reported fewer hospitalizations due to exacerbations in the exercise and PD&P group. Quality of life, ACT preference, and the need for antibiotics were not reported. Exercise versus Underwater Positive Expiratory Pressure (uPEP): One trial with 13 participants compared exercise to uPEP (also known as bubble PEP). No adverse events were reported in either group, but the evidence was of very low certainty. Participants perceived exercise as more fatiguing but also more enjoyable than bubble PEP. No differences were observed in the total weight of sputum collected during treatment sessions. The trial did not report primary outcomes such as FEV1, quality of life, or exercise capacity, nor secondary outcomes like other lung function measures, adherence, need for antibiotics, or hospitalizations. Conclusions: This review highlights the importance of addressing one of the top research questions identified by the CF community: whether exercise is an acceptable and effective ACT and whether it can replace traditional methods. However, the limited number of trials and their diverse designs prevent definitive conclusions. The evidence is of very low certainty, leaving the effectiveness of exercise as an ACT uncertain. Longer-term studies focusing on outcomes that matter most to individuals with CF are needed to answer this question.
